sentences: Across a calm lake, silvery stripes run out in a zigzag.
A small wooded island floats in the distance, and at the very top a thin band of blue sky and bright white clouds.
This is Lake Keitele by the Finnish painter Akseli Gallen-Kallela.
It is painted in oil on canvas, 53 centimetres high and 66 centimetres wide, and was completed in 1905.
The National Gallery in London has owned it since 1999.
Keitele is a remote lake in central Finland.
The painter spent the summer of 1904 on its shores, painting its clear water and brilliant northern light.
Around that time he made four pictures of the lake, and every one of them shows this zigzag pattern on the water.
Look first at the stripes on the water.
They are a natural effect of the wind meeting the lake's currents.
But the painter called them Väinämöinen's wake, the trail left by the singing hero of the Finnish epic Kalevala as he rows across the lake.
The Kalevala, a body of ancient Finnish folk poetry, was first published in 1835.
At the time Finland was an autonomous Grand Duchy of the Russian Empire, and it became independent only in 1917.
For people longing for self-rule, a landscape filled with myth was a way of speaking about the nation.
Look at the water in the foreground at the bottom.
Unlike the broad, flat bands further out, here the shimmering ripples are painted realistically.
In places the bare canvas is left showing, adding texture and light.
Now look at the broad blue-grey bands crossing the lake.
They are treated almost as a flat design.
It is a deliberately archaic style, shaped by Gauguin's decorative abstraction and by Finnish folk art, and it recalls stained glass and textiles, both media he also worked in.
Find the wooded island and the horizon far away.
We are not standing safely on the shore but looking straight out over the water.
That is why, on such a small canvas, the space feels as if it opens out without end.
The artist was born Axel Gallén in Pori, Finland, in 1865.
He studied in Paris and became a pioneer of a distinctly Finnish national art through his paintings of the Kalevala.
In 1907 he officially changed his name to a Finnish form, and he died of pneumonia in Stockholm in 1931.
In a letter to a friend he described the silver stripes on the still water as small waves heralding a storm of feeling yet to come.
In a landscape with no figures at all, only this trace tells us that someone has passed by.
Step back and look again.
Still water and moving wind, an ancient song and the dream of a new nation share one small canvas.
Think back over the path you took today, and whether someone had left a trace on it before you.
